# Amazon DynamoDB: say it

<!-- speak:start id=dynamodb-s01 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** On-demand or provisioned capacity? I do not know my traffic yet.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Start in on-demand mode. It bills each request and needs no forecast. Move to provisioned capacity when traffic is steady and predictable.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: start in on-demand mode, and decide again later.

It works like this. On-demand is the default, and AWS recommends it for most workloads.

You don't set any capacity. You pay for each read and write request.

A table with no traffic pays nothing for throughput.

With provisioned capacity, you set the reads and writes per second. You pay for that capacity every hour, used or not.

Provisioned suits steady traffic that you can forecast.

The thing to watch is a very big spike.

On-demand instantly handles up to double your previous peak.

Before a launch far above that, you pre-warm the table.

You can switch modes later, so this choice is not final.

In your case, on-demand fits a new pipeline with unknown traffic.

What does your busiest hour look like after the launch?

**Skeleton.** on-demand first / pay per request / double the previous peak / provisioned when traffic is steady

**Must say.**

- On-demand mode is the default and recommended throughput option for most DynamoDB workloads.
- On-demand mode bills per read or write request, and a table with zero traffic is not charged for throughput.
- Provisioned mode charges for the hourly capacity you provision, not what you consume, and suits consistent or predictable traffic.
- On-demand instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak traffic; pre-warm the table before a bigger event.

**Do not say.**

- "On-demand has no limits, so it absorbs any spike.". Say: On-demand instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak traffic on a table. For a bigger event, pre-warm the table.
- "Provisioned capacity is always cheaper.". Say: Provisioned capacity suits consistent or predictable traffic. For spiky traffic that you cannot forecast, on-demand is the better choice.
- "After you choose a mode, you can never switch back.". Say: You can switch from on-demand back to provisioned at any time. Switches from provisioned to on-demand are limited per rolling day.

**Follow-up questions.**

- How often can we switch between the two modes? From on-demand back to provisioned, at any time. From provisioned to on-demand, up to four times in a 24-hour rolling window.
- Doesn't auto scaling make provisioned capacity safe for spikes? Not fully. Throttling can occur even with auto scaling, because auto scaling does not respond instantly and stops at the maximum capacity you configure.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=dynamodb-s02 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** DynamoDB or PostgreSQL: which database should our new app start with?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Both work well on AWS. DynamoDB fits known key lookups at any scale. PostgreSQL fits joins and queries you can't predict yet.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both are good databases on AWS. The difference is how you ask for your data.

It works like this. DynamoDB is a key-value database with no servers to manage.

It gives single-digit millisecond performance at any scale. In on-demand mode, you pay for each request.

But it has no joins. You design the table from the questions it must answer.

PostgreSQL is relational. It runs SQL with joins, so you can ask new questions later.

On AWS, that's Amazon RDS or Aurora.

The thing to watch is a new access pattern in DynamoDB.

A question you didn't plan for can need a new index or a redesign.

In your case, list the queries your app runs most often.

If each one looks up items by a key, DynamoDB is a strong fit.

Which of your screens needs data from several tables at once?

**Skeleton.** how you ask for data / key lookups at any scale / no joins, design for questions / list your top queries

**Must say.**

- DynamoDB is a key-value, serverless, fully managed NoSQL database with single-digit millisecond performance at any scale.
- DynamoDB doesn't support a JOIN operator, unlike relational databases.
- In DynamoDB, know the questions the table must answer before you design the schema.
- A relational database such as Aurora fits less predictable query patterns and complex queries through joins.

**Do not say.**

- "DynamoDB supports joins, like SQL.". Say: DynamoDB doesn't support a JOIN operator, unlike relational databases.
- "With DynamoDB, you don't need to plan your queries up front.". Say: Know the questions the table must answer before you design the schema, and design it to make the most common queries fast.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can we use both in one product? Yes, per workload. DynamoDB for key-value lookups at any scale. A relational database such as Aurora for joins and less predictable query patterns.
- What if we need a new query on an existing DynamoDB table? You can add a global secondary index to an existing table to query by another key. A local secondary index can be created only together with the table.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=dynamodb-s03 -->
### Prompt 3

**A customer asks.** Our DynamoDB table shows spare capacity, but some writes are throttled. Why?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** One partition key gets most of the writes. Each partition has its own ceiling, so that partition throttles while the others sit idle.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: one hot key is hitting the ceiling of one partition.

It works like this. DynamoDB hashes the partition key to choose a partition.

Each partition has a fixed ceiling of reads and writes per second.

When most writes go to one key, they all land on one partition.

That partition is throttled, while the others stay underused.

The thing to watch is the key design, not the table total.

Choose a key with many distinct values, so writes spread out evenly.

Or add a random suffix to a busy key, to split its writes.

The throttle reason in the error shows when one partition is the cause.

In your case, we can check which key values get the most writes.

Is there one customer or one item that is much busier than the rest?

**Skeleton.** hash picks the partition / each partition has a ceiling / hot key throttles alone / spread the key

**Must say.**

- DynamoDB feeds the partition key value into an internal hash function, and the output decides the partition of the item.
- Every partition delivers at most 3,000 read units per second and 1,000 write units per second.
- Concentrated traffic above the partition limits is throttled while other partitions stay underutilized: a hot partition.
- Spread the writes with a partition key that has many distinct values, or add a random suffix to the key values.

**Do not say.**

- "Raise the table's capacity and the throttling stops.". Say: A hot partition is throttled at the partition limit while other partitions stay underutilized. Spread the key instead.
- "Switch to on-demand mode and the throttling goes away.". Say: Every partition is designed to deliver at most 3,000 read units per second and 1,000 write units per second.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Doesn't DynamoDB fix a hot key by itself? Partly. Adaptive capacity rebalances partitions so that frequently accessed items don't reside on the same partition. A key with many distinct values is still the main fix.
- How do I know that one partition is the problem? The throttling exception gives the reason type KeyRangeThroughputExceeded when individual partitions exceed their throughput limits.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

### Prompt 4

**A customer asks.** If the AWS Region we use goes down, do we lose our job records?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** DynamoDB replicates each record across three Availability Zones, and a confirmed write is durable. A full Region outage needs a second copy in another Region.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: one failed data center loses nothing, but a Region outage stops access.

It works like this. A Region is one AWS location with several separate data centers.

Each group of data centers is called an Availability Zone.

DynamoDB copies every write to three Availability Zones in our Region.

When DynamoDB says a write succeeded, it's stored durably.

We can also turn on continuous backups, so we can restore a table.

The thing to watch is a whole Region going down.

Then we wait for it to come back.

A global table keeps a live copy in a second Region that takes reads and writes.

That second copy costs extra every month.

In your case, I'd add the second Region when a customer contract requires it.

How many minutes of downtime can your customers accept?

**Skeleton.** three Availability Zones / a write is durable / Region outage stops access / global table for a second Region

**Must say.**

- DynamoDB synchronously replicates data across three Availability Zones in an AWS Region.
- A write that returns HTTP 200 (OK) has completed and been durably persisted.
- Point-in-time recovery gives automatic continuous backups of a table.
- In a global table, any replica table can serve reads and writes, and no database failover is needed.

**Do not say.**

- "DynamoDB copies our data to another Region automatically.". Say: DynamoDB replicates data across three Availability Zones in one Region. A copy in another Region needs a global table.
- "Our backups keep us running during a Region outage.". Say: Backups let you restore a table. To keep serving during a Region outage, a replica table in another Region serves reads and writes.

**Follow-up questions.**

- How fast would the second Region take over? With a multi-Region eventual consistency global table, you can achieve an RPO of a few seconds and an RTO of zero. A global table has no primary Region, so no database failover is needed.
- Can a backup bring back records that someone deleted? Yes. Point-in-time recovery keeps automatic continuous backups. A restore creates a new table, because you can't overwrite an existing table during a restore.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->
